title: Hubble snaps images of a pinwheel-shaped galaxy
caption: The face-on spiral galaxy NGC 1309, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 1309 · constellation Eridanus · about 100 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, The Hubble Heritage Team, (STScI/AURA) and A. Riess (STScI)

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: The NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope photographed NGC 1309, a spiral galaxy that faces us nearly head-on so its arms can be seen in full. The galaxy lies 100 million light-years, or 30 megaparsecs, from Earth.
NGC 1309 does not live alone. It is one of about 200 members of the Eridanus group of galaxies, a loose gathering of galaxies held together by their mutual gravity.

The galaxy also hosted a stellar explosion. Light from the supernova SN 2002fk reached Earth in September 2002. A supernova is the violent death of a star, and for a while it can shine as brightly as a whole galaxy of ordinary stars. The face-on angle gives Hubble an unobstructed look at the galaxy's disc, recorded here in color.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.87 x 2.67 arcminutes) and distance (100 million light years), the frame spans roughly 83,000 × 78,000 light-years. Its light set out about 100 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 1309 in visible and near-infrared light through filters at 435, 555 and 814 nm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.
